articles.title: India's opposition parties march to top court as protests over voter lists escalate
articles.summary: Opposition parties say revisions to the list of eligible voters favor Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party. Authorities have removed more than 130 million names from the voter roll.
body: NEW DELHI — India's opposition parties marched to the Supreme Court on Monday to protest a purge of voter lists they say favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, after police detained thousands of activists over the weekend in a sweeping crackdown in New Delhi.
Several opposition lawmakers and thousands of supporters marched through the capital and submitted a petition to the chief justice alleging irregularities in the nationwide revision of voter lists.

Protests led by the "Cockroach" youth movement have intensified since election authorities began the revision last year, removing more than 130 million voters from the lists. The protesters, including opposition parties, are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Critics say the process is politically motivated and risks disenfranchising eligible voters. Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny allegations of manipulation, saying the move is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible names.
Ahead of the march, authorities closed six metro stations in the capital on Monday and warned of traffic disruptions.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party described the growing protests as a fight to defend the constitution.
"We will not back down," he told reporters in New Delhi.
Gandhi, scion of India's most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn the protests into a broader challenge to Modi.

Gandhi briefly rode through the crowd in an open bus, waving a copy of India's Constitution. Thousands of his party supporters, student activists and other protesters followed in tow. The turnout marked a sharp contrast with the weekend, when authorities briefly detained thousands, including leaders of the "Cockroach" movement and journalists, and effectively locked down much of the capital to prevent large-scale protests.
Modi has not publicly commented on the protests, but leaders of his party have dismissed them, with some calling the activists "anarchists."

Meanwhile, New Delhi police announced Monday that Jantar Mantar, a longtime site of mass protests in the capital, would no longer be a designated venue for rallies. Police said three replacement sites had been chosen.
The "Cockroach" movement earlier this year staged a sit-in at Jantar Mantar that lasted for weeks, forcing the resignation of Modi's education minister in July.

articles.title: DOJ launches antitrust probe of TV networks. And, Trump says Ukraine needs new leader
articles.summary: The Justice Department is investigating several TV networks for possible antitrust violations. And, President Trump pressures Ukrainians to elect a new leader.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

President Trump is urging Ukrainians to hold wartime elections and replace President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as he blames him for not ending the war. He accuses Zelenskyy of causing rising global fuel prices due to Ukraine's long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel on Friday temporarily, and stated both sides agreed to an "energy ceasefire."

The Justice Department has opened a formal antitrust investigation into five major U.S. television networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News — for their actions during a legal battle over access to the White House. Press rights groups have denounced the move, which comes after Trump barred CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House, citing unfair negative coverage. The administration revoked White House press passes for more than 70 journalists. The affected news organizations have sued to restore their access. The Justice Department is citing national security grounds for its actions, while a federal judge has temporarily ordered the restoration of their passes, with a final decision expected by Tuesday evening.

NPR confirms that at least four people died from storm-related incidents after Hurricane Isaias struck the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm on Friday night. Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are assessing the damage and power outages caused by the storm. Isaias brought 105-mph winds, snapping trees and knocking out power, while officials warn of ongoing flash-flood threats farther inland.

Houthi forces in Yemen are attacking Saudi airports, including a deadly strike on a passenger terminal in the capital, Riyadh. Saudi Arabia says at least 20 people have died from these recent attacks in the last week.

Suicide is a growing public health crisis in the U.S., especially within the Black community, where rates have increased more than 50% in the last decade, according to CDC data. Black youth suicides by firearms surpassed those of white youth in 2022. As public health initiatives increasingly pull away from issues that affect different communities, Morning Edition's Michel Martin wanted to address this issue with care and honesty. Martin led a live event titled Going There: A Matter of Life and Death, uniting clinicians, lawmakers, and individuals affected by this epidemic to try and find out why this crisis is happening, how it affects us and how we can take action. The speakers included influential voices like CEO emerita of BET Debra Lee, Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-NJ, psychiatrist Dr. Paul Nestadt, retired NFL champion Vernon Davis, WWE superstar Ettore "Big E" Ewen and Rev. Johnny Parker, who is both a pastor and a counselor. Watch and listen to the event here.
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can reach someone 24 hours a day, just to talk or to help get access to care.

BTS frontman RM is showcasing art from his personal collection for the first time in a collaboration with the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. The K-pop idol's real name, Kim Nam-joon, has prompted the group's fanbase, known as ARMY, to coin the term "Namjooning" to describe the star's interests. RM collaborated with two of the museum's curators for the exhibit RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me. The works on display feature mostly RM's own art collection alongside works from SFMOMA, like a Mark Rothko painting, shown side by side with one by Yun. The museum's director of retail Shane Salvata says, "This is hands down the most inventory that we've ever front-loaded for an exhibition." If you can't visit the exhibit in person, check out some photos of what's on display.
This newsletter was edited by Christina Romano. Suzanne Nuyen contributed.

articles.title: Russia hits Ukraine gas facilities after Trump claims 'energy ceasefire'
articles.summary: Trump said he had brokered a cease-fire to protect energy infrastructure in Russia and Ukraine. But Ukrainian officials say bombs kept falling overnight on gas facilities, wounding 33 people.
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Russia continued missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, hours after President Trump claimed that Moscow had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" designed to spare energy-related infrastructure in Russia and Ukraine.

"We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities," Zelenskyy said on the social media platform X. "I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump. And the message from Russia was very clear — they don't know anything about the energy ceasefire."

According to Zelenskyy, a jet-powered Iranian "shahed" drone fired from Russia struck a gas production facility around midnight, while other drones struck at least five other energy-related targets. He said 33 people were reported wounded across the country.
Later on Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine supported the concept of an energy ceasefire, but he called for more pressure on Russia "for de-escalation to actually succeed."
"Russia must take corresponding steps. As of now, there is no indication that Russia is complying with the conditions outlined by the American President," Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post.

On Sunday, Trump said on his social media platform that "both parties" had agreed to the partial ceasefire, adding, "Do not break it!" He offered no details about the arrangement. But officials in Moscow appeared to show little willingness to limit strikes.

Asked about the energy ceasefire on Monday, Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov rejected the idea as another attempt by Zelenskyy to exploit a proposed pause in the fighting to regroup and rearm. "I do not think [Zelenskyy] deserves a respite," he said.

NPR asked the White House for comment on Russia's overnight strikes and what they mean for Trump's proposed ceasefire. Administration officials have yet to respond. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has often targeted civilian infrastructure, including gas and electric systems.

Trump's efforts to broker a deal protecting energy infrastructure in the warring nations comes amid rising fuel prices in the U.S., following Trump's decision to go to war with Iran. Gas prices have emerged as a major challenge for Trump and his Republican allies ahead of next month's midterm election.

Last week, Trump announced a controversial plan to reduce diesel prices by reviving imports from Russia. On Sunday, however, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators released a statement calling Trump's proposal unlawful.
"Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine," the statement said.

Zelenskyy and many U.S. allies have supported the idea of an energy ceasefire, while condemning Trump's plan to import Russian diesel. Zelenskyy called Trump's move a "weak decision," while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sunday the move is "in direct opposition" to international peace efforts.

In a statement Monday, Trump described his effort to partner with Russia to lower U.S. energy prices as a part of his "America First" strategy, prioritizing U.S. interests over concerns about Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
"The European Union paid Russia $250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story. I made the right choice for the American People," Trump wrote.

Russia's official news agency TASS confirmed Monday that Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has agreed to supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. in October, with monthly supplies increasing in the months ahead.
"The US administration, in turn, issued a general license authorizing Russian diesel supplies to the global market until April 7, 2027," TASS reported.

While Ukrainian officials say they have so far respected Trump's call for an energy ceasefire, they did strike large data centers inside Russia operated by Yandex, a company often described as Russia's version of Google. The strike led to service outages in parts of Russia.

Zelenskyy said Monday that the strikes on Yandex have also led to a drop in the number of Russian propaganda bots appearing on social media. "A lot of people noticed it. There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations," he said.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV to undergo lung surgery this week
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV said he would undergo surgery after doctors found a "localized nodule" in his lung.
body: Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he would have surgery this week to remove a "localized nodule" in his lung.
Leo said the nodule was found at a "very early stage" with doctors recommending surgery.
"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," Leo said during his weekly Sunday noon blessing in St. Peter's Square.
The surgery will take place at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which is the primary location for popes to receive medical attention.
"I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers," Leo said to the crowds on Sunday. He later posted the message about his surgery on social media.

According to the American Cancer Society, a lung nodule is a small abnormal area, less than or equal to 3 cm, found during a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. These tests are often conducted as routine screenings for "trauma, heart disease, non-cancer related lung disease, or lung infection."
Dr. Panagis Galiatsatos, a pulmonary physician at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, said lung nodules are common in older adults.
"The majority of lung nodules are benign," Galiatsatos said. "I usually call them the lungs' wrinkles"
When they're discovered, doctors will test them to determine whether there is cause for concern.

"If they're now discussing that they need to remove the lung nodule, one of his tests must have crossed their threshold … and the suspicion and concern for cancer became a little bit higher," Galiatsatos said. "So that's why he's undergoing this surgery."
Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said in a statement that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week."
Leo's next major international trip is scheduled for early November to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear if the surgery would affect his itinerary.
During his papacy, Leo has been outspoken about peace throughout the world. He spent part of his Sunday address renewing calls for peace in Ukraine.
"I make a heartfelt appeal to the parties to the conflict to allow the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea," Leo said. "The daily bread of millions of people cannot be held hostage by war."
On Saturday, the Pope also called for the death penalty to be abolished, saying on X that it is "inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person."

"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption," Leo said.

articles.title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
articles.summary: Despite the US president announcing energy infrastructure would not be targeted strikes have continued, Ukraine says.
body: Emergency services responded to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine on Monday
Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".

There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants
Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.
He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities."
"I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.
Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday.
On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.
Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.
Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".
On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district.
Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured.
Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire claim mean for Ukraine?

When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".
Asked about the ceasefire on Monday, Trump said they agreed "because I said you agree", adding that the war "has to get settled".
"That war is a disaster if you see the numbers," he said.
For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides.

Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".
Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.
In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.

Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.
Energy facilities in Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on Sunday evening, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.
The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.
However, there has been a mixed response among European officials.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."
Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman, BBC Verify

articles.title: Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
articles.summary: While Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggests he would sign up to a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, Russia has said little.
body: Employees of DTEK energy company in Ukraine work to restore power supply following a missile strike in July

On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure "effective immediately". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggested it was "news for me", while Russia has not commented publicly.
Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire has been agreed.
Kyiv asks: Has it? It is willing to sign up – if Russia does.
Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked whether such a ceasefire had been agreed during his daily conference call with journalists.
"Contacts are continuing," Peskov replied.
"As soon as we have anything to say about this, we will definitely inform you."
Peskov may not have had much to say on the matter, but the pro-Kremlin media has.
It has dubbed President Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire "a gift" for Moscow.
"Of course we benefit," pro-government news outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets concluded.
"It means that all Russia has to do is not destroy Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery.
"That has already been attacked several times. It's barely functioning anyway.
"But Kyiv won't be allowed to hit the multitude of refineries we have.
"In effect it's a one-way deal that benefits us. That's why no one here has officially rejected it."
In other words, Moscow believes Trump's announcement ties Ukraine's hands, not Russia's.
In recent months, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities have caused extensive damage, as well as fuel shortages across the country.
Should such attacks continue, expect the Russians to claim that Kyiv is harming US economic interests – as well as the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections in November.
Russian officials will argue that the strikes undermine the recent Trump-Putin fuel deal for the US to import Russian diesel.
Trump has claimed the agreement will benefit US consumers, although there is widespread scepticism that the volumes involved will do much to lower fuel prices.
Vladimir Putin has shown little desire to stop the fighting
Still, the Kremlin will be only too happy if Ukrainian drone strikes on oil facilities spark fury in the White House and curtail US support for Kyiv.
Moscow would welcome Washington cutting off intelligence sharing to Ukraine and weapons sales to Europe that are destined for Kyiv.
It has already delighted to hear Trump declaring: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called for a 60-day Russian ceasefire to allow for presidential elections in Ukraine.
"The Kremlin, the president, has said many times before, we don't want a ceasefire, we want a lasting peace, and we're willing to do whatever's possible for that," Peskov said.
"Whatever's possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, or a 30-day ceasefire, or anything close to that.
On Monday, the Kremlin proposed a one-day cessation of hostilities for Ukraine to hold elections.
That will not be seen in Ukraine, or in the West, as a serious offer.
It comes as no surprise though.
Putin has shown little desire to halt the fighting.

Recent statements, speeches and signals from Russia's leader suggest that, with winter approaching, the Kremlin is counting on a continued campaign of Russian strikes to significantly increase the pressure on Ukraine.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
The Kremlin has claimed to seek "lasting peace" but right now it is continuing the fighting.
On Monday, Zelensky claimed that Russia had hit several energy targets across Ukraine during the night and into the morning.
"This window of opportunity should be used to knock Ukraine back to the Stone Age and force it to accept peace on Russia's terms," the pro-government Moskovsky Komsomolets has written.
The Kremlin's objective hasn't changed: Ukraine's capitulation.
Moscow seems to believe that the diesel deal with Trump and the US president's growing impatience with Zelensky will help Russia secure its goal.

articles.title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds
articles.summary: Backdated paperwork also made the Russian oligarch’s yachts and mansions disappear from accounts, investigation finds.
body: Watch: The documents that were falsified to allow Roman Abramovich to evade tax
The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.
Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.
Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".

Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".
The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.

Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.
The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".
Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.
Chateau de la Croe (top left) in the south of France, Fyning Hill in Sussex and two superyachts vanished from company accounts

The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022.

The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential, external investigation.

In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false.

The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city.

Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune.
The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices.
Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune

He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But what’s the truth about Roman Abramovich’s fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax.
Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October.

Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth.
Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property.

A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus.
Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax

To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003.
Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts.
When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained.
Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading.

Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.
Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.
This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.
It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.
But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.
Abramovich's close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest

An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.
MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.
A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree".
MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.
This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.

Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.
So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.

Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.

Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."

In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.
MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.
It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.

Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.

MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.
Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.

Andrew Mitchell KC told Panorama: "What you take away from it is there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law. And it looks that they will stop literally at nothing in terms of creating documents."

Vladimir Milov, Russia's deputy minister of energy as Abramovich built his empire and now a critic of the Russian government, said: "For each Russian oligarch or Middle Eastern or African corrupt oligarch, there's an army of Western financial and legal services and PR services providers, who is easily taking money for whitewashing their reputation and making them look normal."

Denying any wrongdoing by the oligarch, Roman Abramovich's lawyers said that he was "not involved in the day-to-day operation of those companies" and that where arrangements were proposed by professional advisers, "reliance on that advice was entirely proper and legitimate".
Deloitte Cyprus said it could not comment on the specific allegations because the documents were more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.
MeritServus closed following the Cyprus Confidential leak.

articles.title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
articles.summary: It comes after the armed group hit Riyadh's international airport and another facility, killing 13 people, in a significant escalation.
body: Watch: Footage from inside Riyadh's airport shows the moment the strike hit on Saturday
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.
"The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.

On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.
The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.
The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.
A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.
Explosions were heard again in Riyadh on Monday night, with the Saudi-led military coalition saying a ballistic missile had been intercepted and destroyed.
A Houthi spokesperson said the group had again targeted the airport.
The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.
Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.

Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.
On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
King Fahd International Airport in the north-eastern city of Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.
Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.
In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks.
"You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.
But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".
Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges.
"We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.

On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".
Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.
UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.

President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.

Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.

Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

articles.title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34
articles.summary: Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, starred as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series.
body: RJ Mitte was best known for playing Walter White's defiant son on the Emmy-winning drama Breaking Bad.
US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34.
"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," his representative told the BBC.
He died in Brownsville, Texas. No immediate cause of death was provided.

Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series starring Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. He earned a Screen Actors Guild Award in 2014 for his work on the series.
"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," his representative Sean Reilly said in a statement to the BBC.
Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's.

He created The Mitte Foundation as well, to support philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, using his platform "to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities", Reilly said.
Breaking Bad aired on US cable broadcaster AMC for five seasons from 2008 to 2013.

The anti-hero drama created by Vince Gilligan earned a whopping 58 Primetime Emmy nominations and won 16, including two for Outstanding Drama Series in 2013 and 2014. It is widely credited as being one of the best US TV series of the 21st century.

Cranston plays a high school chemistry teacher in New Mexico who turns to a life of crime to support his family after a cancer diagnosis. As he descends deeper into the underbelly of the meth trade, he drifts further from his son, Walt Jr, who made his displeasure known with levity through much of the series.
The cast of Breaking Bad accepts the top prize for drama at the SAG Awards in Los Angeles in 2014.
Mitte, who grew up in Louisiana, was a young teen when he auditioned for the breakthrough role after moving to Los Angeles to support his younger sister's acting career in 2005.
He has previously said that his first audition in Los Angeles was for a California state public service announcement for an anti-meth commercial.
"Fast forward to auditioning for Breaking Bad, which is still, in my opinion, an anti-meth thing because it doesn't end well for anyone," he said on the Joe Vulpis Podcast earlier this month.
His character was based on Gilligan's late friend with a more severe case of cerebral palsy who used forearm crutches, which Mitte did not require.
He played the role with honesty and accessibility, cracking jokes as a teen whose health condition was never mentioned in the series.
After rising to prominence with the series, Mitte fought for more varied roles and complex depictions of characters with disabilities, both visible and invisible.
"Whenever awards season rolls around, we always hope to see a diverse group of projects that reflect all of us, in body and mind," he told the BBC in 2021.
"Watching the awareness grow around disability representation has been great to see, but breakthroughs sometimes come in pieces and moments instead of larger change," he said.
Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year.

articles.title: South Africa's deputy police chief resigns after being charged with sexual offences
articles.summary: Shadrack Sibiya had denied grooming a 16-year-old and raping an 18-year-old.
body: Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya has denied all the charges against him
South Africa's deputy police chief has resigned three weeks after he was charged with sexual offences.
A lawyer representing Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya submitted his resignation letter at his disciplinary hearing on Monday, a police spokesperson said.
Sibiya, 59, is also accused of having links to organised crime bosses - allegations which led to him being suspended last year.
He denies those allegations, as well as charges that he sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He also faces a charge of human trafficking.
Sibiya says he did have sex with the 18-year-old but that it was consensual.
He has been in custody since he was arrested three weeks ago.

Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said in a post on X that his departure from the police force was regarded as a dishonourable discharge, external because he was still facing a disciplinary case when he resigned.
The accusations that Sibiya was linked to crime bosses emerged at a major public inquiry over allegations of police corruption and collusion with criminals, known as the Madlanga Commission.
Sibiya was accused of interfering with investigations into political killings in KwaZulu-Natal province.
He was also accused of receiving a gift of cash, as well as 20 impalas, from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract.
The Madlanga Commission has transfixed South Africa over the past year and unearthed widespread allegations of links between police officers and crime bosses.
It was set up by President Cyril Ramaphosa after the KwaZulu-Natal police chief held a press briefing where he accused the then Police Minister Senzo Mchunu of working with criminal gangs.
Mchunu denies the allegations against him but has been suspended.

articles.title: Immigration agents search congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
articles.summary: Omar, an outspoken Trump critic, said the search was "an attempt to target political enemies" and she "will not be silenced".
body: Watch: Agents seen outside US Congresswoman llhan Omar's home
US immigration agents have searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar as part of a criminal investigation.
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorised search warrant" for the property in the Washington DC area, a US justice department spokesperson said.

The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation", the spokesperson said, but no further details were given. The US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at home.
Omar, a Democrat and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponise federal law enforcement".
HSI agents loading a box outside the residence
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said in a statement.
"This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said he had "nothing to do" with the justice department's investigation into Omar, while describing her as a "complainer" and a "terrible person".
The Republican president said of the Somali-born congresswoman: "She comes from a country that is a non-country.
"And then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution."
Omar's communications director Jacklyn Rogers called Monday morning's raid "an outrageous abuse of power" by the Trump administration, adding: "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."
The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear.
A BBC crew saw several agents at Omar's home, some carrying boxes to a van.
News of the search was first reported by Fox News, which said the investigation was about immigration paperwork filed by her late father when Omar was a child.
The timing of the raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years - raised concerns from Omar's fellow Democrats.

The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or to disadvantage a candidate.
The US House of Representatives Democratic Party leadership said in a statement that Omar had long been targeted with "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations" by Trump.
"Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," it said.
Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena for her records.
Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", making allegations of marital fraud against Omar.
Separately, White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News that Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.
Omar denied these allegations last month.
"I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email.
Trump has previously suggested that Omar "should go back" to Somalia and that she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House representative.
Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as an "unhealthy and creepy obsession".

The president has also singled out the Somali-American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back".
Some Republicans celebrated the search.
"Nobody is above the law," said Minnesota congressman Tom Emmer. "We look forward to learning more details about this raid and investigation. ACCOUNTABILITY IS COMING!"

Omar is the first Somali American elected to the US House and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan congresswoman Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.
Omar won re-election two years ago with 74% of the vote.
Senior political leaders in Minnesota have criticised the search.
Governor Tim Walz said: "Americans see this for what it is - President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election."
Minnesota senator Tina Smith called it "a transparent attempt to interfere in our elections".
Additional reporting by Ione Wells

articles.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
articles.summary: Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
body: Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.
The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.

More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.

Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process.
Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.
The firm added in s statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date.
"Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to."
The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France.
Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed.
In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon.
The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible".
Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.
As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires.
French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.
Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.

French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".

European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."
In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".
He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".

articles.title: Qantas flight grounded after bedbug outbreak
articles.summary: The flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled after passengers on the plane's previous journey complained of bug bites.
body: A Qantas Boeing 787 Dreamliner (file photo)
A Qantas flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled on Saturday, after an outbreak of bedbugs on the plane.
During the previous flight on Friday - a nearly 17-hour journey from Perth to Rome - some passengers had complained that they were being bitten by bugs, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.
They were reportedly given antihistamines to help ease the itch of the bites, but supplies ran out.
The Boeing 787 Dreamliner had to be grounded for "a deep clean", a Qantas spokesperson told the BBC.

"We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday's Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue was identified on a small number of economy seats," the spokesperson said.
All affected customers were provided with accommodation and were rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, the carrier said.

Bedbugs are small, wingless parasites that can live on clothes, furniture and bedding. Their bites can be itchy but they do not usually cause more serious health problems, the NHS website says, external.

But they can be difficult and expensive to get rid of. Treatment includes washing all bedding, clothing, and household materials like curtains on a hot wash and tumble dry, or they can be put in plastic bags in a freezer for three or four days.
Bedbugs causing travel chaos is not unusual - less than two weeks ago, several Southeastern train services in England were cancelled after drivers discovered the creepy-crawlies in their cabs.
In 2017, British Airways apologised to a family travelling from Vancouver to London, after they were left covered in bug bites from an overnight flight.

And Turkish Airlines faced with a PR nightmare last year after the New York Times reported, external of several instances of bedbug infestations on its planes - and allegations at the time that the airline did nothing about it.

articles.title: Tom Cruise film Digger forecast to become one of Hollywood's biggest flops
articles.summary: The film dropped by around 60% in its second weekend, and could become one of Hollywood's biggest flops.
body: Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance at the box office.
Ticket sales for the satirical black comedy, which stars Cruise as oil magnate Digger Rockwell, dropped by around 60% in the movie's second weekend in cinemas.
It brings Digger's total box office takings so far to around $35m (£26m) globally. The film is estimated to have cost its studio Warner Bros around $280m (£211m) to make and market.

But Cruise said last week, external that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them [in terms of] opening weekend," adding he was instead focused on making films that "hopefully will translate, last and evolve".
The film's box office takings relative to its budget mean it could become one of the biggest film flops in Hollywood history.
That would put Digger in the same bracket as other films which lost upwards of $100m, including 1995's Cutthroat Island, 2002's The Adventures of Pluto Nash, 2005's Sahara and 2012's John Carter.
Other films estimated to have lost nine-figure sums include Mars Needs Moms (2011), Amsterdam (2022), The 13th Warrior (1999), The Marvels (2023) and Speed Racer (2008).
Digger's performance stands in sharp contrast to the success of major franchises starring Cruise in recent years, such as new instalments of Top Gun and Mission: Impossible.
Hollywood trade publication Variety said Digger was expected to end its box office run with around $50m (£38m) worldwide.
The film would need around $350m (£264m) to break even, due to its budget, marketing costs, the portion of ticket sales that go to theatres and the likely spend on an awards season campaign.
However, a Warner Bros spokesman pushed back slightly on the figure, telling Variety the film's break even point was $300m (£227m).
Digger was the last standalone release for the studio before its recent takeover by Paramount.
The film is directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, best known for films such as Birdman, Babel and The Revenant.
Digger received generally poor reviews from critics, prompting Warner Bros to launch a new marketing campaign urging audiences to "decide for yourself".
Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning, starring Mikey Madison and Jeremy Allen White, also performed poorly
Meanwhile, the new sequel to the Oscar-winning hit The Social Network also struggled at the box office on its opening weekend.
The Social Reckoning took $5.5m (£4.1m) in the US, significantly lower than the $22m (£16m) its predecessor took on its opening weekend in 2010, not adjusted for inflation.
Globally, Aaron Sorkin's latest film, starring Mikey Madison, Jeremy Strong and Jeremy Allen White, took around $9m (£6.8m).
The film tells the true story of a Facebook engineer, Frances Haugan, who leaked internal documents to a reporter after becoming concerned about some of the company's practices.

The Social Reckoning was beaten in the US box office chart by horror movie Other Mommy, psychological thriller Verity, video game adaptation Resident Evil and Brad Pitt's wilderness thriller Heart of the Beast.

articles.title: US detains man accused in multi-billion Venezuelan money laundering scheme
articles.summary: US officials had been offering a reward of $10m (£7.5m) for information leading to Álvaro Pulido's arrest.
body: Álvaro Pulido was wanted by US authorities over indictments accusing him of money laundering
A Colombian man wanted for allegedly laundering money that had been illegally syphoned off a Venezuelan government welfare plan has been detained in the United States.

The US Department of Justice said Álvaro Pulido, 62, had been arrested during a Homeland Security Task Force operation on Sunday, but did not provide further details as to how he ended up in US custody.
Pulido had been in jail in Venezuela since March 2023 accused of diverting profits from the state-run oil company PDVSA.
The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and State Department had been offering a reward of $10m (£7.5m) for information leading to his arrest.
He is due to appear in court on Tuesday, according to a statement released by the US Attorney's Office.
Pulido's arrest comes just two months after Alex Saab, another Colombian businessman with close ties to the Venezuelan government, pleaded guilty to money laundering charges in a US court.

The US State Attorney's Office said that Pulido had been charged in two separate federal indictments "involving the alleged laundering of more than $2bn (£1.5bn) in connection with Venezuelan government bribery schemes".
US prosecutors say Pulido, along with four other co-defendants, bribed Venezuelan government officials to secure contracts to provide poor Venezuelans with food and medicine.
They accuse Pulido of wildly overcharging the Venezuelan government and laundering the profits through bank accounts abroad, including in the US.
They also allege that Pulido worked with Alex Saab to launder $350m from a separate bribery scheme involving Venezuela's currency exchange system using bank accounts in Florida.
Until recently, Saab was a powerful figure in the Venezuelan government with close ties to the then-leader, Nicolás Maduro, who named him minister of industry in 2024.
However, after Maduro was seized by US forces in a raid on Caracas in January and taken to New York to stand trial on drug-trafficking charges, Saab's fate quickly changed.
Less than two weeks after Maduro was seized, the new US-backed interim government of Venezuela sacked Saab from his post as minister, and in May it extradited him to the US.
Last month, Saab pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.

articles.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
articles.summary: Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticised the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections.
body: Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February
US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.

Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.
That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.
The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.
As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.

This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.
They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".
The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.
Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.
The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.

Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.
