articles.title: After two tragic incidents in months does safety at English zoos need a rethink?
articles.summary: Even though a man was mauled to death by a tiger and three-year-old was attacked in crocodile enclosure, experts say public protection is robust
body: On a busy Saturday afternoon at a zoo in Yorkshire, visitors looked on in horror as a man climbed into a tiger habitat, minutes after posing for a photograph beside it.
Eyewitnesses said he scaled a metre-high viewing barrier, before dropping into the enclosure below, overpowering a woman who tried to pull him back.
The resident 30-stone Siberian tiger, named Altai, was seen pawing at the man, who was dragged away, and later declared dead at the scene.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park remained closed on Monday, while a City of Doncaster council spokesperson said the local authority had launched a health and safety investigation into the matter.

It marked the second serious incident at a UK zoo in just a few months. In June, a three-year-old boy was seriously injured after being attacked by one or more crocodiles when he ended up in the enclosure at Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire.
But experts have said that recent events do not reflect on zoo practices, and may instead point to issues with human behaviour, or mental health or support services.

“These were two really terrible events, but rather than being about zoos themselves, I wonder whether they could reflect wider issues in society,” said Amy Dickman, professor of wildlife conservation and the director of WildCRU at the University of Oxford.

“Given how many millions of zoo visits there are in a year, these are vanishingly rare instances, although of course that doesn’t negate how deeply tragic they are when they occur,” Dickman, an expert in big cat conservation, added.
“I would not conclude that there was a major issue with zoo safety – the harsh reality is that it is virtually impossible for zoos to stop people who are very determined to breach safety measures.”

In the Cambridgeshire incident, the boy was allegedly thrown into the crocodile enclosure. Police arrested a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder at the time of the incident, and police said he was “assessed as not being fit for interview”.
This week, a spokesperson for Cambridgeshire police said the investigation was still under way and the suspect had been bailed until 17 December.

“Two incidents have happened in the last few months, which is obviously really upsetting and distressing for the sector, but they are actually very, very rare,” Jo Judge, the chief executive at British and Irish Association of Zoos and Aquariums (BIAZA), said.
There are hundreds of zoos, aquariums and animal attractions in the UK, and about 32 million people visit BIAZA member zoos and aquariums across Britain and Ireland every year.

“The industry has already put in place so many safety measures that it is not being seen as a rising problem or something that we’re not doing enough about. These are just very unusual and very rare incidences,” she added.
“It is unbelievable that these two incidents have happened so closely together.”

Dickman said that because animals kept in enclosures do not come into contact with humans as those in the wild may do, “for someone to walk into that environment is probably far more dangerous, ironically, than if you were out in the wild with animals that were used to navigating those spaces alongside people.”

She said she had “never visited a zoo in the UK and thought ‘this is dangerous’,” adding there was “layer upon layer of protection against people interacting with dangerous animals” and that “you do have to do it very intentionally”.

All zoos in the UK must be licensed and follow strict safety procedures to protect their animals and human staff and visitors, with guidelines in place for zoo enclosures, including for sizing and perimeter fences.

“There is no accidental falling into a category 1A dangerous animal enclosure, it just doesn’t happen – it’s not designed that way,” said Campbell Murn, a lecturer in conservation science at University of Reading, who until recently sat on Defra’s Zoos expert committee.
Category 1A refers to a high-risk species kept in zoos that is capable of causing a human fatality, and includes rhinos, elephants, great apes and big cats.

“In terms of preventing intentional entry to enclosures, there’s locks, there’s barriers,” he added. “But short of putting an electric fence [up], which of course has its own health and safety considerations, the protocol remains patrolling staff keeping an eye out for unusual behaviour.
“It’s simply not possible though, at an attraction like Yorkshire Wildlife Park that gets hundreds of thousands – if not over a million – visitors a year to keep an eye on everybody all the time.”

He said safety had to be balanced against visitor experience, so zoo-goers don’t get “a sense of walking into an electrified fence fortress where they can’t do anything other than look through heavy steel bars”, and used the analogy of “a determined thief”.

“If a determined thief wants to get in your house, they’re going to get in your house,” he said. “You can mitigate risk to a certain point but there’s sometimes no stopping events from happening, unfortunately.”
Paul Rose, a senior lecturer in psychology (animal behaviour) at the University of Exeter, also said that “public behaviour can be unpredictable, as we all know”.

“There will be mitigation in place, such as high fencing, standoff barriers, signage and explanation and a code of conduct for how to behave at the zoo (and for visitors to take responsibility for their actions),” he said. “Risk assessments will also be undertaken regularly.”

Following Saturday’s incident, he said he imagined that “lessons will be learned regarding how zoos try to manage the behaviour of the public and how they instruct visitors to conduct themselves in and around enclosures”.

“The majority of visitors behave in a way respectful of the animal and environment at the zoo, but there is always a risk of rogue or unusual behaviour, and this will continue to be risk assessed and part of zoo personnel training,” he added.
Experts did say they had some concerns about the role the internet and social media may play in encouraging people to interact with wild animals.

Judge said: “We do unfortunately see on social media quite often videos of people, mostly in other countries, entering the enclosures with some of these animals, and that is something that we do not support at all.”

“They are dangerous wild animals and they should be respected as such,” she added, but said it wasn’t something UK zoos are “hugely concerned about” as they “will make it very, very clear that these are dangerous animals”.

But Dickman said that online content was definitely of concern. “Though it may not have been a factor here, it is worrying how many videos exist online of people playing around with tigers and lions,” she added.
“AI has made that even worse, and the illusion that people should have those interactions with wild, dangerous animals can be really damaging.”

articles.title: Man rescued from cave on Sardinia after being trapped by rockslide for 26 hours
articles.summary: Luca Olmetto was trapped roughly 10 metres below ground in the Gorroppeddu cave in the Urzulei mountain range
body: A 31-year-old man has been pulled alive from a cave on the Italian island of Sardinia after being trapped roughly 10 metres below ground for 26 hours following a rockslide.

In a huge and complex operation, rescuers worked non-stop after Luca Olmetto became trapped in the Gorroppeddu cave in the rugged Urzulei mountain range in central-eastern Sardinia on Sunday afternoon.

He had been exploring the cave with his girlfriend, who was a few metres behind him and narrowly missed the collapse, which completely blocked the entrance to the cave. She managed to escape unharmed and immediately raised the alarm.

Rescuers managed to reach Olmetto, who was conscious and responsive throughout the operation, by late Monday afternoon after manually removing rubble and earth blocking a narrow passage. They then proceeded with the delicate operation of removing the large amounts of debris that covered the caver before extracting him from the cavity. According to Rai News, Olmetto was brought to the surface just after 6pm CET and stabilised by medical staff before being airlifted to hospital.

About 48 experts from Sardinia’s Alpine and Speleological Rescue Corps and 30 firefighters, as well as civil protection staff, were involved in the rescue operation. A helicopter also provided materials and equipment needed to make the site secure.

In a message posted on social media, the council of Codrongianos, the town in north-west Sardinia where Olmetto is from, wrote that the past 24 hours were filled with “great anxiety for the entire community”.

“We are closely monitoring the situation and are hoping for good news soon,” the council said. “Our thoughts are with Luca and his family, and we extend our deepest gratitude to all the rescuers working tirelessly to bring him to safety. Hang in there, Luca – all of Codrongianos is with you.”
The Gorroppeddu cave is a largely unexplored natural cavity.

In a similar incident in December 2024, another explorer, Ottavia Piana, 32, became trapped while exploring a cave in the Bueno Fonteno caves close to Bergamo in northern Italy. She remained underground at roughly 600 metres for 75 hours before being freed. Piana suffered injuries including fractured vertebrae, ribs and facial bones. Her high profile rescue involved 160 specialists.

articles.title: Zelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continue
articles.summary: Ukrainian leader says he was surprised by Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ announcement, posted as Russian drones hit Kyiv
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to respond to Russia’s continuing attacks on the Ukrainian power grid as European leaders rally around Kyiv amid a feud with Donald Trump over Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries.

Speaking to a gathering of European security officials in Warsaw on Monday, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv would retaliate if strikes on its power grid continued: “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, we will respond.”

On Sunday, Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Kyiv and Moscow that Zelenskyy said neither side had agreed to. On Monday, Zelenskyy said he was “surprised” by the post, which went online while Kyiv was being attacked by Russian Shahed drones.
Russia then launched a “targeted attack” on a Kharkiv power station hours later, as much of Kyiv was plunged into darkness. “It’s clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskyy said.

Russia bombed six energy facilities on Monday, injuring 33 people, the Ukrainian president said. “It is becoming increasingly clear that Russia does not want to agree to the energy ceasefire proposed by the US and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our communities,” he added.

Zelenskyy also suggested that Ukraine’s recent counter-strikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex had reduced the number of bots posting messages in Europe and the US. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations,” he said.

The Kremlin refused to say on Monday whether it agreed with Trump’s Truth Social post, which claimed a ceasefire was “effective immediately”. It also rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal that Russia stop bombing for 60 days so Ukraine could hold a presidential election. Moscow wanted an overall peace deal first, it said, which, for the Kremlin, means Kyiv’s capitulation.

The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday, when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

Both Republican and Democratic politicians have criticised the move, pointing out that the deal violates a US law that blocks Russian energy imports. On Monday Trump defended it. “I made the right choice for the American People – ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” he wrote in a social media post.

Earlier a furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Ukraine has said it is ready to negotiate an energy ceasefire that would take the pressure off its electricity grid before the winter. European leaders have voiced support for Kyiv in its dispute with Washington, saying Russia was responsible for the continuing strikes on energy infrastructure in both countries.

“We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds,” the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said at a meeting of European foreign ministers on Monday. “We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it.”

Ministers from the Baltic states criticised a US decision to lift sanctions on imports of Russian diesel, which had been blocked as part of punishment for Putin launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

“This deal doesn’t help, neither the crisis of the oil products, nor the unity within the transatlantic community when it concerns Russia,” said Lithuania’s foreign minister, Keʂtutis Budrys. “And it is not the European way. Our way is to increase pressure because we already see how it works.”

Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, using jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles ahead of the cold winter months, leading to blackouts and water shortages far earlier in the season than has been usual during the war.
Trump’s proposal was for both sides to halt strikes on oil refineries but Kallas said that deal favoured Russia, which has far more refineries.
The US president has blamed the high price of diesel on Ukraine’s attacks, rather than the global shock to energy markets from the US war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the strait of Hormuz.

According to the Financial Times, the US ⁠has threatened ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons, paid for by its European allies. The White House has also said it could turn off intelligence sharing unless Kyiv halts its ‌long-range strikes on ​Russian oil refineries.

The Kyiv Independent newspaper said Ukraine’s commander in chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, had received a call from the US telling him to stop bombing. “They called all the top military officials with threats,” a Ukrainian official told the newspaper.
Ben Hodges, the former head of US forces in Europe, described the energy ceasefire “deal” as a fantasy and “a classic ‘Trumpian’ announcement of something not based on any facts.”
“No one should be misled,” he said, adding that Russia “never adheres to any agreements unless forced to do so”.

He urged Ukraine’s military to ignore Trump and “ramp up” their attacks on Russian oil and gas complexes. “Clearly, this is having a very significant effect. Otherwise, you wouldn’t be hearing all this pressure from the Kremlin on the White House demanding that it stop. Of course, it is having a huge impact.”

articles.title: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport
articles.summary: Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breaches stretched defences
body: Saudi Arabia has been forced to suspend all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one person dead. Some airlines, including Gulf Air and Bahrain Air, had already said they were cancelling flights until next Saturday. More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabian’s military spokesperson said.

The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.
The country has pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality. But some senior oil executives did not attend or appeared virtually.

The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises. Amin Nasser, the president and chief executive of Aramco, said Saudi Arabia had invested deeply in protecting its supplies, but “no nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone.”
He added: “Markets can diversify suppliers. They cannot diversify geography […] when energy infrastructure in this region is targeted, the consequences reach economies everywhere.”

An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam.

Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country.
Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft.

The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014. Saudi Arabia badly needs stability to continue the slow diversification of its economy from oil dependence, but has not found a way to restore it in Yemen.

Inside Yemen, fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides.

The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services.

Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids on Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada.

On the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi Political Bureau claimed Saudi Arabia accepted the mediation offered by Iran and proposed first a one-month truce, and then a two week truce, but the Houthis had rejected both offers.

He said “the battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena, and the cards have changed. Therefore, a comprehensive settlement must be put in place between Riyadh and Sana’a, the Houthi capital because every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow”.
A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation.

The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates.

The STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state.
Related: The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong | Nesrine Malik
The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades.

Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weaken Donald Trump.

Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including his call for the Ukrainian president to stand aside showed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. You can see for yourself what America’s friendship and enmity with its allies is like.”

articles.title: Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises
articles.summary: US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies
body: Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.

Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000).
Related: Nobel prize for economics awarded to two Americans, Hall and Woodford, for work on New Keynesian models – business live

“New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said.

These models improved on John Maynard Keynes’s stabilisation models, which struggled to handle the impact of the oil shock in the 1970s, when countries suffered high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment at the same time.
Related: John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis
Hall and Woodford demonstrated how traditional models could be reconstructed, based on how individual households and businesses collectively affect an economy through their actions.

Hall’s work was based on forward-looking consumer behaviour rather than the more mechanical rules of thumb used by Keynes, which linked key variables such as inflation, unemployment and gross domestic product (GDP).
Woodford built on this work to create the New Keynesian model, a full macroeconomic stabilisation framework that is the main tool for policymakers now.
This model was used after the 2008 financial crisis by policymakers as they steered the global economy away from the risk of a second great depression.

“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, the chair of the committee for the economics prize, said.

Hall and Woodford’s work also led to the development of forward guidance, where central bankers communicate where they expect interest rates to be in the future. That became an important tool after the 2008 financial crisis, and the Covid pandemic, when interest rates were cut to record lows.

Forward guidance has had its critics, though – the current chair of the US Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, has argued it should only have a “limited and circumscribed” role in normal times, to avoid “creating ambiguity in the name of clarity”.
And in 2014, the then Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, was labelled an “unreliable boyfriend” for dropping hints over interest rate rises that never came to pass.
Woodford said he was “elated”. “It’s a tremendous honour. It’s a surprise but I’m feeling very good about it,” he told reporters in Stockholm by phone after receiving the news.
The Columbia University president, Jennifer L Mnookin, said: “I offer my deepest congratulations to Michael Woodford on this tremendous honour.

“What a tribute to his groundbreaking work alongside Robert E Hall that has fundamentally reshaped the theoretical foundations of stabilisation policy and provided us with the tools to navigate economic upturns and downturns more effectively.”
Hall is also known for coining the idea that US economists can be divided into freshwater and saltwater varieties.

The fresh water group, who tend to be based at inland universities located near the Great Lakes, such as the University of Chicago, believe in free markets, neoclassical price theory, rational expectations and monetarism.

Salt water economists, though, cluster at coastal universities, such as Harvard, MIT, UC Berkeley, Yale, Princeton, UCLA and Columbia. They tend to be Keynesians and New Keynesians, believing that governments and central banks can affect demand in their economies.

The economics Nobel prize is not one of the five created by Alfred Nobel. Instead, it was invented by Sweden’s central bank, and is known as the Sveriges Riksbank prize in economic sciences in memory of Alfred Nobel.

articles.title: Fire destroys Marché des Enfants Rouges, ‘coolest market in Paris’
articles.summary: ‘A lot of sadness’ after 17th century landmark that escaped demolition in the 1980s goes up in flames
body: Fire has ravaged Paris’s oldest surviving covered food market, a popular street food venue dating back to the 17th century in the Marais district of the French capital that drew thousands of locals and tourists daily.

Ariel Weil, the central Paris mayor, ​said the Marché des Enfants ‌Rouges had been “totally destroyed” in the blaze, which broke out soon after 3am. “The worst was avoided: the fire did not spread to the surrounding buildings,” he said. “But there is a lot of emotion. A lot of sadness.”

The market was established in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII and took its name from a nearby orphanage, the Hospice des Enfants Rouges – founded in 1536 by King Francis I and his sister Marguerite de Navarre – whose child residents were habitually dressed in red.

The structure was listed as a historic monument in 1982 but narrowly escaped demolition shortly afterwards when Paris city hall, led by the then mayor, Jacques Chirac, approved radical redevelopment plans that would have replaced it with an underground car park, a council daycare facility and community centre.

A determined campaign by local residents and neighbourhood associations, backed by intellectuals, writers and artists including film-makers and photographers such as Bertrand Tavernier and Willy Ronis, who captured its traders on camera, gathered tens of thousands of signatures in protest and the plans were eventually abandoned in the mid-1990s.

Rather than demolish the building, the city undertook a six-year, 13m-franc (about €3m, or £2.5m today) renovation project, restoring the market’s historic wood and ironwork frame and glass roof. Les Enfants Rouges reopened as a food court in 2000.

While still hosting some traditional stalls including a greengrocer, butcher, cheesemonger and fishmonger, the 1,000 sq m market was mostly given over to more than a dozen stands offering French, Lebanese, Moroccan, Japanese and other street food at the counter or at casual chairs and tables.

The current Time Out tourist guide describes Les Enfants Rouges as “the coolest market in Paris”, while the authoritative US website Food&Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year after other food courts in London, Bangkok, Lyon and Mexico City.

Lt Col Pierre de Bouvier of the Paris fire service said much of the metal structure of the market had fallen in, and most of the stalls had gone up in flames. More than 150 firefighters and 50 fire trucks battled the blaze after being alerted at 4.15am, he said, adding that the cause of the fire was not yet known.

articles.title: Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?
articles.summary: Attacks by Iran-backed group come amid counteroffensive by Yemeni government supported by Riyadh
body: On Saturday, a missile strike by the Houthis in Yemen hit Riyadh’s international airport, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. On Sunday, another attack ‌killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.
CCTV footage showed people cowering at the moment of impact of Saturday’s attack.
Footage filmed in the aftermath of showed damage inside one of the terminal buildings at the airport, which is located about 22 miles north of the Saudi Arabian capital.
The attacks by the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, were the biggest escalation yet in their campaign ⁠against Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in recent weeks.
Though the violence might appear at first sight to be restricted to the Arabian peninsula, it could have global consequences, pushing up fuel prices and so international inflation.
The Houthis’ timing is partly opportunistic but also rooted in the dynamics of the conflicts across the Gulf.

The Houthis initially stayed on the sidelines of the conflict launched by the US and Israel against Iran earlier this year. But last month, the Islamist militia movement seized control of key territory and gained virtual control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, which dominates the Red Sea, a critical shipping route for oil and gas exports from the region.
The Yemeni government forces and local allies began a major counteroffensive last week to drive back the Houthis from the Bab al-Mandab and also hit other Houthi positions.

Saudi Arabia is in the Houthis’ crosshairs because it supports Yemen’s UN-backed government and its forces. Their attacks on high-profile targets in the kingdom such as oil infrastructure and the capital’s airport – key symbols of its international integration and economic future – makes painfully obvious the costs of Riyadh’s strategic choices.

Such attacks also benefit Iran, which has long supported the Houthis as part of its “axis of resistance”, a coalition of Islamist hardline movements that allows Tehran to project power and influence round the region.

The new threat from the Houthis to the Red Sea and to Saudi Arabia highlights again the massive leverage Tehran and its allies can exert on global oil and gas supplies, countering recent US pressure in bold move on the conflict’s chessboard.
The recent attacks on Saudi Arabia have been the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade.

They also marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi civil aviation in years, forcing airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services. Businesses in Riyadh’s financial hub have told employees to work remotely, authorities in Riyadh have asked schools to switch to online classes this week, and top energy executives were ⁠dropped from the schedule of a high-profile conference this week in the capital.

Though Saudi Arabia has intervened indirectly in conflicts around the Middle East and beyond for decades, violence has rarely struck the kingdom itself. In recent months, the country has found itself on a frontline, something its rulers have long sought to avoid.
Saudi Arabia has invested enormous sums in its military – the kingdom is the world’s eighth biggest spender on weapons – but Houthi attacks are very hard to stop.

“Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves,” said Thomas Juneau, a security analyst at Ottawa University.
Other analysts point out that even the vaunted Israeli air defence systems failed to stop a ballistic missile narrowly missing Ben Gurion international airport last year.

Reprisals against the Houthis and efforts to pre-emptively destroy the movement’s offensive capabilities are not easy either. The US bombardment in 2025 showed how hard it is to destroy the militia’s capabilities, which have been much enhanced over recent years, in part through Iranian advice and investment.

The Houthis say their actions were “guided by reciprocity” – suggesting they are responding to ongoing Saudi strikes on the territory they control in Yemen – but show no sign of stopping their attacks.
“Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing,” official statements carried by the Houthi-run al-Masirah television channel said.

It seems unlikely Saudi Arabia will halt its counterstrikes, and equally unlikely the kingdom will be able to find a way to block all incoming Houthi missiles, though it may improve its intelligence gathering and early warning to allow better defence of specific high-value targets.

Nor is there any imminent prospect of an end to the hostilities between Iran and the US that are a major factor in the surge of the recent violence in Yemen. And though the Houthis are more a coalition of different factions than a coherent single movement, for the moment they appear unified behind hardline and ideologically committed leaders.
Farea al-Muslimi, a specialist on Yemen and the Gulf at Chatham House in London, said the Houthis had been consistently underestimated over the years.

“They have really upped their game and believe they can get something now which will reposition them within the region. They are very confident at the moment and feeling empowered …. But though they think they can control this [escalation], that may well be an illusion,” he said.

articles.title: Former Irish Olympic swimming coach and child abuser George Gibney jailed for 15 years
articles.summary: Gibney, 78, has faced justice for abusing athletes in the 1970s and 80s after decades of effort to track and extradite him
body: More than half a century after he started sexually abusing children, and enjoyed prestige as Ireland’s Olympic swimming coach before fleeing to the United States, George Gibney has faced justice.
The 78-year-old was sentenced to 15 and a half years in prison at the central criminal court in Dublin on Monday for abusing four young female athletes in the 1970s and 1980s.
It was the culmination of a decades-long effort by victims, police, journalists and others to track down and extradite Gibney from the US.
He was convicted in July of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape after a closely watched trial that detailed harrowing abuse.

Judge Micheál P O’Higgin called Gibney a “manipulative predator” who had insinuated himself into the lives of children under his care. “It was predatory in nature and a gross breach of trust,” he said. “He used his coaching role to access and assault defenceless children under his care.”
The judge said Gibney had once enjoyed a stellar reputation and that the sentence reflected the gravity of his offending. “From these heights he has fallen, and his reputation now lies in tatters.”
The former coach, seated in a wheelchair, showed no emotion.
Speaking to reporters outside the court, Orla Poole said she had spent “decades in silence” because of his actions. “I thought I was the only one, that somehow, I deserved what he did to me.”

She said other survivors should know that they were not alone and could seek support. “The only guilt for what we went through lies with the convicted paedophile. When you are ready and able, unburden yourself by talking to someone from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, One In Four, a therapist, a trusted friend or even the gardaí.”

Evin Daly, a child welfare advocate who helped to find Gibney in Florida, said the sentence was vindication for Gibney’s victims. “The abuse shaped some of their lives. The guy had no conscience, in my opinion.”

Ireland had little international success in swimming in the 1980s but Gibney became a high-profile, respected figure for establishing the Trojan club in south Dublin and for coaching emerging talent at pools around the city. He was Ireland’s coach for the Olympic games in Los Angeles in 1984 and Seoul in 1988. Gibney urged his swimmers to “never give up” and to “hang in there”.

After allegations emerged that he preyed on children at pools, in his car and other locations, he was charged with 27 counts of indecency and carnal knowledge, but in 1993 the supreme court ruled that he could not face trial because of the time that had elapsed since the alleged offences, a decision that stunned his victims.
Free but infamous, Gibney moved to Scotland, then the US, where he obtained a visa and built a new life, living in Colorado, California and Florida and working mostly in low-level clerical jobs.
Several journalists continued to dig into Gibney’s crimes, including Justine McCarthy of the Irish Times who wrote a 2009 book, Deep Deception.
Related: Gary O’Toole: 'There are people like George Gibney in every sphere of society' | Donald McRae
Daly, a forensic sociologist who was then the chief executive of a child protection advocacy group called One Child International, helped the media to locate and keep tabs on Gibney.

“We provided data and resources,” said Daly, a Florida-based court consultant on child welfare cases. “At one point Gibney moved because his neighbours in the apartment complex got wind of the fact that he was an accused sex offender and they turned on him.”
In 2020 a 10-part podcast series, commissioned by the BBC and presented by Mark Horgan, titled Where is George Gibney? revived attention and scrutiny.

Four victims who were minors when they were abused made statements to Irish police between 2020 and 2022, leading to fresh charges, an extradition warrant and Gibney’s arrest and return to Ireland last year.
After the conviction in July four victims told the court of the impact of the abuse.
One said she retained “intensely personal and traumatic memories” and had harboured a “secret shame, hurt and bewilderment” for more than half a century. The abuse was a “frozen nightmare”, she said.

Another victim, who was nine at the time of the assaults, told Gibney in court that he had abused his position of trust and that her burden of shame, guilt and embarrassment was now his. Gibney had presided over “the destruction of a previously happy and healthy child” who was powerless to verbalise her torment, she said.

• In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International

articles.title: German minister quits after ‘indecent’ attacks intensify during bereavement
articles.summary: Fragile coalition suffers another blow as labour minister and co-leader of SPD Bärbel Bas leaves both posts
body: Germany’s labour minister and co-leader of the centre-left ⁠Social Democrats (SPD), Bärbel Bas, has quit both posts, citing the death of her stepdaughter and subsequent political attacks against her, in a stinging blow to the fragile coalition government.
“After my stepdaughter’s death, I realised that I need time to come to terms with my grief,” Bas said in a statement posted on Facebook, without giving further ⁠details.

Explaining her departure from frontline politics, Bas explicitly blamed public broadsides against her as she grappled with the family tragedy, “unfortunately also from among the ranks of the coalition partner [Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)]”.
She said the attacks “continued to intensify during this difficult time for me personally”.

Some CDU lawmakers had criticised Bas’s absences during a crunch phase of an economic reform drive seen as crucial to the teetering government’s survival, although it was widely known she had experienced a death in her immediate family.

Bas’s co-leader at the SPD, Lars Klingbeil, who is also Merz’s vice-chancellor and finance minister, expressed regret at her departure and criticised the sniping against her while she was mourning as “indecent”.
Klingbeil cancelled a planned trip to India to deal with the fallout from Bas’s resignation, and complained about a degradation of the national political discourse.
“We are ​competitors, and we need ​a culture ‌of debate. ​But ​we also need a culture of mutual respect,” Klingbeil told reporters.

Merz, who has been fighting for his political survival after three disastrous state elections for his CDU last month, thanked Bas for “cooperation based on trust” in government and offered his condolences.
“As a father and grandfather, I can only imagine how deeply felt this loss is for you. I wish you and your family strength,” he wrote on X.

Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, also gave Bas her sympathies but said her angry words towards the CDU demonstrated that Merz’s coalition government “is at its end”. She added: “We need a fresh start for Germany.”
The AfD, Germany’s biggest opposition party, is leading national opinion polls at about 30% after a strong showing in September’s regional elections, which also resulted in gains for the hard left.
Bas, who will remain an MP for Duisburg in the former Ruhr mining region, is a former president of the Bundestag lower house of parliament and one of the most experienced members of the SPD.
Her ministry oversees large parts of Germany’s costly social welfare system, which Merz has targeted for cuts.

While a representative of the party’s left wing, Bas was widely seen as a constructive team player able to bridge the kind of implacable policy disputes that have plagued Merz’s government since its inception in May 2025.
Her absence will now be keenly felt.

The coalition is deeply divided over plans to revive the sputtering economy, the EU’s largest, with Merz spearheading a pro-business savings drive and the SPD insisting on maintaining protections of workers’ rights and benefits.
The pension system is in particularly urgent need of reform as German society rapidly ages but plans to gradually lift the retirement age have met with angry resistance.

Approval ratings for Merz and his government have plunged over the course of the year, with voters fearing further deindustrialisation in the face of Chinese competition and steep rises in the cost of living.
Merz, a former corporate lawyer, is often perceived as haughty and out of touch, compounding his administration’s woes and giving rise to calls to replace him at the helm.
He has vowed to stay in office and fight for his policy agenda, saying it was the only way to beat back the “poison of authoritarianism” with extremists on the march.
The next general election is due in 2029 but five more state polls loom next year.
One of Merz’s cabinet ministers, Karin Prien, sounded the alarm last week, publicly calling for a change of course in the CDU away from Merz’s harsher stances and rhetoric.

“We bit our tongues for two or three years but that’s no longer an option,” the family affairs minister told Reuters ahead of a weekend party leadership meeting, referring to its centrist wing. “The ‘pure CDU’ approach (pursued by Merz) has failed.”

articles.title: Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive
articles.summary: Naffah Naffah makes the bells in the mountains near Beirut. His sons will take over the foundry when he retires
body: The story of Lebanon’s last remaining church-bell maker begins with a rifle. In the 18th century, Youssef Gabriel, a local metalworker, was secretly making and equipping Arab revolutionaries with rifles to assist their revolt against the Ottoman empire, which controlled Lebanon at the time.
Then, one day, a Russian engineer came to the Lebanese town of Beit Chabab to make a church bell. Gabriel, intrigued, shadowed the man and picked up the process on sight.

Or, another story goes, the Maronite patriarch at the time, frustrated by the Ottoman empire blocking the import of church bells to Mount Lebanon, tasked Gabriel with making a bell. After several attempts he succeeded and decided to give up making arms, converting his gunsmithery into Lebanon’s first church-bell foundry.
Where the stories converge is that the village, impressed with Gabriel’s handywork, rechristened him Youssef Naffah – naffah meaning useful or successful in Arabic.

Three centuries later, the Naffah family is still making church bells in Beit Chabab. Once one of 10 bell foundries owned by the family, the workshop operated by the master bell-maker Naffah Naffah and his two sons is the last remaining production centre for church bells in Lebanon. It is also the sole source of church bells for much of the Middle East and even Lebanese diaspora communities in Europe, Australia and the US.
Naffah, 57, said: “We have to pass it down to our kids, it’s been 300 years. I didn’t have any choice. My own father, he would come to the workshop when he could barely even walk.”

The foundry sits under his home on the edge of a hill overlooking the red tiled roofs of Beit Chabab and the Lebanese coast that stretches beneath it. The picturesque town, in the Mount Lebanon range about a 30-minute drive from Beirut, offers an escape from the city’s chaos and a refuge from the violence of the country’s last two wars.
The ceiling and walls of the foundry are blackened from decades of smoke that has belched from the furnace, and the floors are cluttered with bells in various stages of construction.

Outside are mounds of white clay mixed with goat hair, each layer drying before the next is applied. The final product forms the interior mould that the molten metal is poured around. Inside the workshop, modern tools mix with the ancient, a hydraulic press sitting next to a well-worn anvil placed on top of a tree stump.

Each bell takes about two months to make. It takes about 40 days to make the interior mould and another month to create the outer mould, with crosses, decoration and the workshop’s signature imprinted on the white clay as it hardens.

The third and final stage is the quickest: a foundry is heated using burning wood, and a mixture of copper and tin is placed inside to be melted down over 24 hours. When the metal is ready, it is poured over the bell mould, hardening within three minutes.

The workshop produces about 25 bells a year, about 20 of which go to churches in Lebanon. The cost of the bell depends mostly on the size, with every 100kg (220lbs) costing $8,000 (£6,000). A medium-size bell that is ready in the foundry and weighs about a tonne costs about $80,000.

“I hate giving the bells away, it always makes me upset, like I’m giving away a child,” said Naffah. He pointed to a mould being worked on, imprints of crosses on its clay interior. “Look at this bell, it’s the work of my two hands. I’ve poured my heart and soul into it.”

Each bell bears the names of those who worked on it. One bell ready to be installed has the name of Naffah, his son Charbel and the patron who commissioned it. Other bells in the shop for repairs – one from 1910, another from 1932 – bear the names of Naffah’s grandfathers.

The family maps Lebanon by its churches, finding evidence of their ancestors up and down the small Mediterranean country. The earliest surviving bell that bears their name is in the town of Qalaat Sahyoun and was forged in 1725.

The ringing of the bells is part of daily life in the villages that wind through Lebanon’s mountains and dot its sprawling coast; on a Sunday morning, the sound mingles with the chirping of the birds.

During the Hezbollah-Israel war in Lebanon, which reignited in March, the Christian villages of south Lebanon were cut off from the rest of the country. Israel’s ground invasion, which bulldozed dozens of villages in south Lebanon, mostly spared the Christian villages, but it left them isolated.
The church was a crucial source of comfort for the besieged Christians. It organised the distribution and transfer of aid in and out of towns and across frontlines when necessary.

Naffah, Charbel and his other son Youssef are determined to preserve this Lebanese tradition and their place within it. Charbel will succeed his father as the master of the family workshop, and Youssef helps when he is not busy with his studies at medical school.
Youssef said if Charbel ever decided he no longer wanted to make bells, he would leave medical school and take his place as master of the foundry.

“We have six churches in the village [Beit Chabab]. If all of the bells played at the same time, I could distinguish between each one from their sound alone,” he said, surveying the village from the edge of the foundry. “Traditions are important to us. We are living and breathing tradition here in this workshop.”

articles.title: Melbourne Islamic leader rejects centre’s alleged Flydubai hijacker links after Facebook video
articles.summary: MyCentre leader Samir Mohtadi, who also goes by Abu Hamza, says claims associating him with flyDubai pilot are unfounded
body: The leader of a Melbourne Islamic centre allegedly linked to the accused Flydubai hijacker has rejected any connection with the radicalised pilot, saying he never met the suspect, and condemned “violence in all its forms”.

The UAE government has alleged that investigators had traced the ideological and professional background of the 29-year-old suspect, Omani national Hammam al-Hammami, and that his “drift towards extremism and terrorism” began while a student at RMIT University in Melbourne in 2017.

The UAE’s attorney-general stated al-Hammami, had said that while studying in Melbourne he regularly attended a mosque affiliated with RMIT, and through those visits had become acquainted with people associated with a centre known as “MyCentre”.

He allegedly said that the centre was managed by a man known as “Abu Hamza” but it was not stated whether the suspect had ever met Abu Hamza. There was no allegation that anyone at the centre was involved in radicalising al-Hammami or had kept in contact with him or had any knowledge of his intentions before the 30 September flight.
In a statement issued late on Monday, Samir Mohtadi – who also goes by Abu Hamza – said al-Hammami was unknown to the Multicultural Youth Centre (MyCentre).
“I have never met Al-Hammami, who has been referred to in recent media reports, and we have no record of him ever attending our centre.
“I strongly reject any attempt to associate me or Multicultural Youth Centre with Al-Hammami.
“Such claims are unfounded, misleading and risk unfairly damaging the reputation of an organisation that has served the wider Australian community for decades.”

Mohtadi said MyCentre had provided community services, including education, gyms, sporting facilities, aquatic and medical centres, and spiritual support for the wider Melbourne community over decades.
“Our doors are open to everyone, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, with hundreds of people visiting our facilities every day,” Mohtadi said.

“Throughout my life, I have consistently preached peace, and both my work and the work of the centre have always focused on promoting peace, harmony, mutual respect and community wellbeing. We unequivocally reject violence in all its forms.”
Related: Flydubai co-pilot began radicalisation in Australia, UAE prosecutors say
On Sunday night, Mohtadi appeared in a four-minute video released on the centre’s Facebook page.

He referred to Islamic texts on the virtues of staying silent when being attacked by others but makes no reference in the video to the alleged Flydubai hijack attempt, the UAE attorney general’s statement or to al-Hammami
“You’ll find those who are righteous you’ll always find have been attacked, abused, accused, killed, imprisoned, and this is the way it is,” Mohtadi said in the video.
“The best thing, sometimes, is not to say anything.”

RMIT has confirmed al-Hammami had studied engineering at the university, but left Australia before completing the qualification. He subsequently underwent flight training in New Zealand and became a qualified commercial pilot.

Passengers and crew on the 30 September flight, which had 182 people onboard, intervened to stop the alleged attempt to hijack the plane and crash it into Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv in a “premeditated terrorist plot”, according to the UAE attorney general’s statement.
According to the statement, al-Hammami allegedly told prosecutors he adopted ideas advocating violence and terrorism and drew inspiration from the 9/11 terrorist attacks of 2001.
“The idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking,” the statement said.

Al-Hammami allegedly prepared himself psychologically and physically to carry out the alleged terror plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach.

Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country, with New Zealand authorities also examining his time there between November 2018 and May 2019.

On Sunday, Australia’s home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said the co-pilot was allegedly radicalised online. He also said the government wanted to properly screen people at the border and in online settings.

articles.title: French centre left must wage ‘existential battle’ to prevent far right winning presidency
articles.summary: MEP Raphaël Glucksmann issues call after becoming social democrat candidate for 2027 presidential election
body: The European lawmaker Raphaël Glucksmann has urged the French centre left to wage an “existential battle” to prevent Marine Le Pen’s far right winning the 2027 presidential election after he was chosen as the social democrat candidate for the presidency.

“We’ve got to rid our hearts of the spirit of defeat,” Glucksmann, the founder of the small party Place Publique, said on Monday morning after his decisive win in a centre-left primary race held by the Socialist party.

In his first interview since being designated a presidential candidate on Sunday night, Glucksmann told France Inter radio that the country was living in a “historic moment”, with the far right at the gates of power. He said the 2027 presidential election campaign would be brutal and “like no other we have ever experienced”. He said it would be unbearable to have a centre left “that doesn’t believe in victory”, adding that he could restore a “pride in social democracy”.

At present the centre left sits substantially behind the far right in the polls and also trails the radical left politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is polling high but with whom Glucksmann refuses to work.

Glucksmann, 46, an essayist and intellectual who argues he is very different to career politicians, is staunchly pro-Europe and pro-Ukraine. His candidacy marks the first time the Socialist party will not have its own presidential candidate since the party was founded in 1969. The party suffered two crushing defeats in the last two presidential elections.

Glucksmann has been a member of the European parliament since 2019. He strikes a more reformist and centrist tone than the Socialist party, but has cooperated with it in the past, presenting joint electoral lists. He has made no secret of his presidential ambitions but needed the Socialist party machine behind him for his campaign.
Glucksman is polling at between 9% and 14%, well behind the frontrunner, Le Pen. He also trails the centre-right contender Édouard Philippe, who served as prime minister under Emmanuel Macron.
Crucially, he is also behind Mélenchon, whose party, La France Insoumise, boycotted the Socialist primary and has presented itself as the biggest force in a divided left.

Glucksmann is tasked with regaining centre-left voters who jumped ship to support Macron, though his critics on the left accuse him of being too centrist. He said the French president, who is standing down next spring, “wasted 10 years” failing to act on the climate emergency.

Glucksmann is known for being a campaigner on international issues. He took part in documentary work to raise awareness of the aftermath of genocide in Rwanda and is a former adviser to the anti-Moscow former Georgian president Mikheil Saakashvili.

Glucksmann, who has been accused by opponents of being too much of a Paris intellectual, said he “lost sleep at night” worrying about how the social-democratic left had lost the working class in France. He said the centre left needed to regain “a form of radicality that we lost” and the focus of this would be environmental policy.
He told the daily Libération he made no apology for being an intellectual and would use his background to “better explain the moment we’re living in” rather than relying on “slogans”.
Glucksmann’s partner, Léa Salamé, is the star presenter of the French public broadcaster’s flagship evening news programme. She has stepped down from presenting the news while he runs for president.

articles.title: Monday briefing: What will it take to turn around our struggling education system?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: With attendance and engagement declining and growing pressure on pastoral care, helping young people rediscover their love for learning requires a new lesson plan
body: Good morning. I’m back, but don’t get too excited. I’ll just be making guest appearances here and there.

Now, on to children, who – if the steady stream of warnings is anything to go by – are in serious trouble. There’s the pull of addictive screens, a sharp drop in children reading for pleasure, a global decline in academic performance, and a notable rise in youth mental health struggles. Together, these trends point to a wider crisis in learning.

Much of the focus has been on phones and social media. A global study published last week found an association between increased screen exposure and lower academic achievement and poorer language development in children. In the UK, phones are already banned during the school day, and from spring of next year, under-16s will not be able to access major social media platforms such as TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram.

But are we focusing on the wrong thing? Today, I speak to Jenny Anderson, award-winning journalist and author of The Disengaged Teen, about why so many young people are disengaging from learning, and what it might take to turn that around. That’s after the headlines.
Ukraine | Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.

Middle East | A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people.

UK politics | Andy Burnham is facing questions over plans to speed up sweeping changes to Britain’s electoral system amid speculation that some of his closest advisers are pressing for an early general election.
Djibouti | At least 139 people, including 15 children, have died after a boat carrying 305 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.
Brexit | Andy Burnham has said it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, after seeking answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 vote when he entered Downing Street.
There is a real and growing crisis in young people’s engagement with learning.

According to recent research, fewer pupils now say they find school engaging. In 2020-21, 42% of students said they found what they learned interesting either “always/very often” or “quite often”. By 2023, that figure had fallen to just 28%. Nearly half of pupils do not take part in extracurricular activities, while severe absence – defined as missing more than 50% of school sessions – are on the rise in England.

Pupils are also becoming less happy at school. The share of pupils who say they are happy at school dropped from 65% in 2020-2021 to 50% in 2023-2024. Perhaps most strikingly, survey data suggests pupils feel worse, physically and mentally, than they did during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Jenny Anderson argues this points to something more complex than distraction from phones: a fundamental problem in how our schools are designed.

“We’re shuffling kids through a system, which they tell us feels like prison,” Anderson explains, adding that young people are “bored to tears by content that feels irrelevant to them”. The consequences of disengagement can extend beyond the classroom. “If they can’t figure themselves out as learners, they often can’t figure themselves out as people. They often don’t feel they belong.”
Much of the debate has centred on the addictive nature of smartphones, particularly the social media platforms that dominate them.

In March, a US court found Meta and Google’s YouTube liable for deliberately designing addictive products used by millions of young people. A flurry of lawsuits against Meta followed, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, around alleged social media addiction in young users.
In August, as part of a landmark $18bn settlement, the company agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, such as a daily usage limit of two hours and blocking social media use at night.
“Phones have done tremendous damage,” Anderson says. “They are very risky to kids because they are clearly created with pathologically addictive algorithms.”
Anderson argues that these algorithms displace the experiences kids need to build a sense of identity and purpose: time with friends, developing interests, and getting involved in their communities.
The platforms are also built around “weaponised engagement”, Anderson adds, putting them in direct competition with the slower and more difficult work of learning.
But while she welcomes the effort to rein in the damage caused by phones, she warns against treating phones as the sole issue in this education crisis.

Anderson describes technology as an “exacerbator” – one which accelerates the disengagement that is already present in schools, rather than causing it in the first place. Phones offer an easy, addictive alternative to the hard work of learning, but simply taking devices away does not automatically re-engage students.
“Focusing only on phones and tech misses the whole story. It distracts us from the conversation about what schools need to fix.”
Anderson’s book investigates why so many young people dislike school, and what can be done about it. She identifies four modes in which students approach their education:

• Passenger: Students who are coasting along and doing the bare minimum. This is about 50% of students.• Resister: Students who withdraw or act out. These are learners dubbed the “problem children”, but they are actually just children struggling with problems.• Achiever: Students who aim to get gold stars in everything without knowing why. They have the highest rate of mental health challenges of all the modes.• Explorer: Students who are curious, self-aware and driven. They have agency: the ability to set a goal, and the skills and will to go after it. While achievers may appear to represent the pinnacle of academic performance, Anderson argues that it’s actually the explorer mode.

These dynamic modes aren’t fixed, Anderson argues. They work in tandem with a set of variables, such as how a student feels about a subject, whether they have had breakfast that morning, or whether they’re fighting with their family.
According to her research, just 4% of children say they spend time at school in explorer mode.
“The irony is that kids who are coasting and appear to be lazy and appear not to be doing what we want often need more autonomy, not less,” Anderson says.

She points to research into what is known as “autonomy-supportive teaching”, which included 35 randomised controlled trials across 18 countries. These studies suggest that giving students greater agency, can improve both academic performance and wellbeing.

Anderson argues schools also need to adapt to how students engage with learning, particularly when the curriculum leaves pupils feeling overwhelmed and disconnected. “Students go through a packed out curriculum that culminates in preparing to sit for 25 exams over two months for their GCSEs,” she says.

Part of the answer lies in giving pupils more agency – this time in the classroom. Rather than assigning every student the exact same essay, teachers could offer a choice of topics and let students pursue the angle that interests them most. The aim is not to lower standards, she argues, but to create forms of learning that compete more successfully for students’ attention.

The pressures on schools may also grow as the climate crisis intensifies. Last week Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union , said schools should consider changing start and finish times, reordering holidays and moving exams from the summer months in an effort to adapt to the UK’s increasingly severe heatwaves. His comments followed school closures during June’s heatwave, which left at least 760,000 pupils in England and Wales missing lessons.

Parents looking at recent headlines about education may feel powerless, Anderson says, but she believes they have a crucial role to play in helping children stay curious and engaged outside the pressures of the classroom.
Her advice is simple: start by asking children what they’re actually interested in.

“I really do think parents play a profound role here, and I think we feel trapped,” Anderson says. “We feel like we have to play the game of the system” – focusing relentlessly on grades, exams and measurable achievement – “but the system is not serving our kids.

“So we have to ask: are we just going to shove them into that system, or help them succeed in that system while also helping them figure out who they are, what they care about, where they want to make an impact in the world?”
When asked what advice she would give to education secretary Lucy Powell, Anderson highlights three priorities, starting with reforming the exam timetable.
“Tests are an excellent way you figure out if kids are learning, but they do not have to be so high stakes,” she explains. “They can be adaptive.”

Her second priority is making the curriculum more relevant to pupils’ lives outside school. “Kids ask all the time, ‘Why do I have to learn this?’ and we do not honour that question,” Anderson says. Schools need to help pupils see the bigger picture.
Her third piece of advice advice would be to reinvigorate the arts and humanities.
While she understands the economic case for the “relentless pursuit of Stem (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics)”, she believes that something vital has been lost.
“What about the humanities? What about the arts, such as drama and music?” she asks. “That is the canvas on which many kids will show up and find their place in school.”

Anderson accepts that learningmust be challenging and rigorous. But, she says, it doesn’t have to be dreary . “There’s a myth of misery, that school can only be good if it’s hard in that joyless way, and that teenagers are just [naturally] unhappy.
“To borrow a Britishism, that’s poppycock.”
